Equivalence, non-inferiority and minimal-effect tests

Source: R/equivalence.R
usdt_equivalence.Rd

Tests interval, one-sided and point hypotheses about the quantities of the three uSDT hypotheses in a frequentist hsdt() fit or a custom model fitted with lme4::glmer(): the difference between mean sensitivities (diff, H1, reported as \(\Delta d'\), influence minus awareness), their correlation (rho, H2) and the slope and intercept of the latent regression (slope, intercept, H3). The hypotheses are written as in usdt_bf(), so a frequentist and a Bayesian analysis can state the same bounds.

Usage

usdt_equivalence(
  fit,
  hypothesis,
  awareness = "d_A",
  influence = "d_I",
  alpha = 0.05
)

# S3 method for class 'usdt_equivalence'
print(x, digits = 3L, width = 80L, ...)

Arguments

fit

A frequentist hsdt object, with or without the replicates of usdt_boot(), or a glmerMod from lme4::glmer().

hypothesis

Character vector of hypotheses. It has no default: the bounds are the smallest effects of interest, which only the analysis can set. Each one is "<quantity> <op> <value>", where the quantity is diff, rho, slope or intercept and the operator is =, < or > (<= and >= are read as < and >), or "<quantity> in [a, b]" and "<quantity> out [a, b]" for a region and its complement.

awareness, influence

For a glmerMod, the fixed effects of the awareness and influence sensitivities, as in usdt_tests(). Defaults match the internal naming of hsdt().

alpha

Significance level of every test, between 0 and 0.5 (default 0.05).

x

A usdt_equivalence object.

digits

Number of decimals printed.

width

Width of the printed report, in characters.

...

Ignored.

Value

An object of class usdt_equivalence: a data frame with one row per hypothesis and the columns hypothesis, test ("Two-sided test", "One-sided test", "Equivalence test (TOST)" or "Minimal-effect test"), H1, H0, estimate, se, conf.level, conf.low and conf.high (the interval that decides the test), ci_method, p.lower and p.upper (the one-sided p-values at the two bounds of a region), p.value, decision, status and reason. Rows that cannot be estimated have status = "not estimable" and give the reason. It prints one report per hypothesis.

The tests

A point statement names the null hypothesis H0. An inequality or a region names the alternative H1, as in usdt_bf(). Each test rejects H0 at level alpha:

  • q = c: the two-sided test of H0: \(q = c\).

  • q > c and q < c: one-sided tests. With a margin on the unfavourable side of the reference value, diff > -0.2 is a non-inferiority test and diff < 0.2 a non-superiority test.

  • q in [a, b]: an equivalence test by two one-sided tests (TOST, Schuirmann, 1987. Lakens et al., 2018). H0, \(q \le a\) or \(q \ge b\), is rejected when both one-sided tests reject their part of it, so p.value is the larger of p.lower and p.upper.

  • q out [a, b]: a minimal-effect test. H0, \(a \le q \le b\), is rejected when either one-sided test rejects it at alpha / 2, so p.value is twice the smaller of p.lower and p.upper. As the region shrinks to a point it becomes the two-sided test of that point.

Each test is decided by the position of a confidence interval, and the row reports that interval: of level 1 - 2 * alpha for the one-sided and equivalence tests, and 1 - alpha for the two-sided and minimal-effect tests, which split alpha between two tails. With the default alpha = 0.05, an equivalence test reports a 90% interval, and H0 is rejected exactly when that interval lies inside the region.

The correlation

The bounds of rho are given, and its estimate and interval reported, on the correlation scale. The test runs on the Fisher-\(z\) scale, where the sampling distribution of the estimate is closer to normal: $$z = \frac{\mathrm{atanh}(\hat\rho) - \mathrm{atanh}(c)}{SE / (1 - \hat\rho^2)}.$$ Because atanh() is increasing, \(\rho > c\) and \(\mathrm{atanh}(\rho) > \mathrm{atanh}(c)\) are the same statement, so the p-value and the decision are those of the hypothesis about rho, and the interval, transformed back, stays inside (-1, 1).

Every p-value comes from the interval reported with it. usdt_tests() instead tests a null association on the covariance that rho and the slope share, so its p-values for rho = 0 and slope = 0 can differ slightly from these.

The intercept and the slope

Both divide by the variance of the awareness sensitivity. When the awareness sensitivity barely varies across subjects, their standard errors are large and their Wald intervals inaccurate, so their equivalence tests need many subjects to succeed, and the bootstrap of usdt_boot() gives more accurate intervals.

Boundary fits and the bootstrap

The correlation, slope and intercept need the full covariance matrix of the fit, which is unavailable when the sensitivity covariance is on the boundary (a variance estimated as zero, or a correlation of -1 or 1). Their rows are then marked "not estimable", while the difference, which only needs the fixed effects, is still tested. After usdt_boot(), every test uses the bootstrap replicates and the interval type chosen there. The p-value at a bound is the share of the bootstrap distribution beyond it, counted as \((k + 1) / (B + 1)\) as in usdt_boot(), so the decision agrees with the reported interval up to that correction.

References

Lakens, D., Scheel, A. M., & Isager, P. M. (2018). Equivalence testing for psychological research: A tutorial. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(2), 259-269. doi:10.1177/2515245918770963

Schuirmann, D. J. (1987). A comparison of the two one-sided tests procedure and the power approach for assessing the equivalence of average bioavailability. Journal of Pharmacokinetics and Biopharmaceutics, 15(6), 657-680. doi:10.1007/BF01068419

See also

usdt_tests(), usdt_boot(), usdt_bf()

Examples

d <- usdt_data_tasks(
  awareness = vadillo_awareness,
  influence = vadillo_cuing,
  subject_col      = "subj",
  condition_col    = "condition",
  condition_levels = c(signal = "old", noise = "new"),
  response_col     = list(awareness = "judged.old", influence = "rt"),
  response_levels  = list(awareness = c(signal = 1, noise = 0),
                          influence = c(signal = "faster",
                                        noise = "slower")),
  dichotomize      = list(awareness = FALSE, influence = TRUE)
)

m <- hsdt(d)

# Mean sensitivities equivalent within 0.2 d' units, and an unconscious
# effect at zero awareness smaller than 0.2
usdt_equivalence(m, c("diff in [-0.2, 0.2]", "intercept < 0.2"))
#>  uSDT hypothesis ─ Equivalence test (TOST)
#> ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
#>   Hypothesis (H1)             : Δd' in [-0.2, 0.2]
#>   Hypothesis (H0)             : Δd' out [-0.2, 0.2]
#>   Estimate                    : -0.107
#>   Standard error              : 0.035
#>   90% CI, Wald                : [-0.165, -0.049]
#>   p-value, lower bound        : .004
#>   p-value, upper bound        : <.001
#>   p-value                     : .004
#>   Decision (alpha = 0.05)     : H0 rejected, in favour of H1
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#>  uSDT hypothesis ─ One-sided test
#> ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
#>   Hypothesis (H1)             : intercept < 0.2
#>   Hypothesis (H0)             : intercept >= 0.2
#>   Estimate                    : 0.045
#>   Standard error              : 0.116
#>   90% CI, Wald                : [-0.146, 0.235]
#>   p-value                     : .090
#>   Decision (alpha = 0.05)     : H0 not rejected
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# The bounds of the correlation are correlations
usdt_equivalence(m, "rho in [-0.3, 0.3]")
#>  uSDT hypothesis ─ Equivalence test (TOST)
#> ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
#>   Hypothesis (H1)             : rho in [-0.3, 0.3]
#>   Hypothesis (H0)             : rho out [-0.3, 0.3]
#>   Estimate                    : 0.491
#>   Standard error              : 0.519
#>   90% CI, Fisher-z            : [-0.528, 0.930]
#>   p-value, lower bound        : .108
#>   p-value, upper bound        : .631
#>   p-value                     : .631
#>   Decision (alpha = 0.05)     : H0 not rejected
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
